clinicalPearls: Results from inhalation of gastric contents, most often during induction, emergence, or in patients with impaired airway protection
Chemical injury from acidic gastric fluid produces a rapid inflammatory pneumonitis, which is distinct from later bacterial aspiration pneumonia
Risk is highest with a full stomach, delayed gastric emptying, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, obesity, reflux, and emergency or difficult airway situations
Signs include hypoxaemia, wheeze or bronchospasm, cough, tachypnoea, and diffuse crackles, sometimes with visible gastric material in the airway
Immediate management is to position to limit further soiling, apply suction, secure the airway, and provide oxygen and supportive ventilation with lung-protective strategies
Routine antibiotics and corticosteroids are not indicated for pure chemical pneumonitis; antibiotics are reserved for established infection or high-risk contamination
Prevention centres on appropriate fasting, rapid-sequence induction with cricoid pressure in at-risk patients, and airway protection with a cuffed tube
Aspiration prophylaxis with agents that reduce gastric volume and acidity may be considered in high-risk patients
reference.pathophysiology: Aspiration occurs when protective airway reflexes are obtunded, allowing gastric contents to enter the tracheobronchial tree. Acidic fluid causes rapid chemical burn of the alveolar-capillary membrane, triggering an inflammatory cascade with increased permeability, alveolar oedema, surfactant dysfunction, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch that produces hypoxaemia. Particulate matter can cause mechanical obstruction and atelectasis. The initial insult is sterile, but secondary bacterial infection may supervene, and severe injury can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome. Severity depends on the volume, acidity, and particulate content of the aspirate.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia
Chest radiograph or CT to identify infiltrates, often in dependent lung zones
Bronchoscopy to clear particulate material when obstruction is suspected
Sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage culture if secondary infection is suspected
Serial observation for progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome
redFlags: Witnessed massive aspiration with rapid desaturation and airway soiling
Progressive hypoxaemia or rising oxygen requirement suggesting evolving acute respiratory distress syndrome
Haemodynamic instability or the need for escalating respiratory support
reference.prognosis: Mild chemical pneumonitis often resolves within days with supportive care, but large-volume acidic or particulate aspiration can cause severe respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and death.
pitfalls: Giving prophylactic antibiotics and steroids for uncomplicated chemical pneumonitis
Underestimating aspiration risk and omitting rapid-sequence induction in at-risk patients
Attributing hypoxaemia solely to aspiration and missing another cause
Failing to protect the airway promptly and allowing continued soiling
Assuming a normal early chest radiograph excludes significant aspiration
management: Immediate airway management with head-down or lateral positioning, suctioning of the airway, and tracheal intubation with suction to limit further soiling
Supplemental oxygen and lung-protective ventilation for hypoxaemia and respiratory failure
Flexible bronchoscopy to remove aspirated particulate material when large-airway obstruction is suspected, rather than routine lavage
Avoidance of routine antibiotics and corticosteroids in pure chemical pneumonitis, reserving antibiotics for established secondary infection or grossly contaminated aspirate
Close monitoring with serial oximetry, blood gases and imaging for progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome, escalating to critical care as needed
Perioperative prevention including appropriate fasting, rapid-sequence induction and aspiration precautions in high-risk patients
